messages.content: Write a conference talk abstract for a talk about moving a monolith to microservices. Around 200 words.

**Title:** Forty Services Later: We Only Needed Six

Three years ago, billing was 900,000 lines of Java, one release a week, and a 51-minute test suite that caught nothing. It's 40 services now. My guess is that 34 of them were a mistake.

This is the boring account of how that happened. I'll cover the three extractions that earned their keep (payments, notifications, the fraud scorer) and the numbers that backed them: p99 latency, release cadence, and how many people had to be in the room to ship one change. Then the failures. Spreading the customer record across four services burned eight months and left us with a distributed transaction we still paper over using a nightly reconciliation job.

You'll go home with one question to ask about every proposed service: which team owns it, and which deploy does it unblock? If you can't answer both, don't cut there. Service boundaries are org boundaries with a network hop stapled on, and a hop you didn't need is just latency plus more pages at 3am.

Find me in the hallway and tell me I'm wrong. I've flipped positions on this twice already.

Substitute your own figures. The shape carries over, but it's the specifics that get an abstract past a program committee.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

**Title:** We Built 40 Services. Six Were Worth It.

Billing used to be 900,000 lines of Java on a weekly release train, guarded by a 51-minute test suite that never once caught a real bug. Today it's 40 services. I think 34 of them were a mistake.

There's no triumph arc here. I'll walk through the extractions that paid off (payments, notifications, the fraud scorer) and show the evidence behind each: p99 latency, release frequency, and the headcount required to get one change out the door. Then the wreckage. Splitting the customer record across four services cost us eight months and produced a distributed transaction we still patch over with a nightly reconciliation job.

You'll leave with one test to run on every service someone proposes: name the team that owns it, and name the deploy it unblocks. If you can't do both, don't cut there. Service boundaries are org boundaries with a network hop bolted on, and a hop nobody needed is latency plus extra pages at 3am.

Come argue with me in the hallway. I've changed my mind on this twice already.

Swap in your own numbers. The skeleton travels, but the specifics are what gets an abstract past a program committee.
